newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa job creation continues slow - bank.
newsitem.headline: South Africa job creation continues slow - bank.

text.p: The recovery in overall economic activity since the middle of 1993 had failed to improve employment growth in the South African economy, the Reserve Bank said in its latest quarterly bulletin.
It said average annual employment in the formal non-agricultural sectors of the economy increased only once during the past six years, rising at a year-on-year rate of 0.7 percent in 1995.
This increase was followed by a sharp decline of 3.6 per cent, at a seasonally adjusted and annualised rate, in the first quarter of 1996 and a further decline of 2.1 percent in the second quarter.
The bank said since the end of the 1980's most businesses had focused on improving productivity to meet the challenges of the increasingly competitive international economic environment.
"Faced by persistent demands for higher real wages and salaries, producers responded by retrenching workers and introducing more capital-intensive methods of production."
The outcome was a decline in aggregate employment instead of in the level of real wages, the bank said.
Real wages, it said, had in fact risen since the end of the 1980's while total employment had fallen.

Total employment by private-sector organisations in the formal non-agricultural sectors of the economy declined consecutively by seasonally adjusted and annualised rates in the four quarters since the third quarter of 1995.
But the bank said total employment in the public sector showed virtually no sign of a reduction in overall size as envisaged in the government's recently adopted macroeconomic strategy.

It said the recent decrease in employment in the formal sectors of the economy led to a rise in the number of registered unemployed workers, bringing the total number of the registered unemployed to almost 320,000 in June 1996 from 244,000 in October 1995.
Labour productivity rose in line with a general upward trend in real wages, rising 3.3 percent last year -- the highest year-to-year growth since 1978 when a rate of 3.9 percent was registered.
Productivity growth came to 2.6 percent in the year to the first quarter of 1996.
"This improvement was partly at the expense of employment and was not entirely accounted for by an increase in work effors," the bank said.
This led to low rates of increase in the nominal unit labour costs in the non-agricultural sectors of the economy from 9.0 percent in 1994 to 5.9 percent in 1995.
